newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Ringgit hits new 42-month low, but recovers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ringgit hits new 42-month low, but recovers.

text.p: The Malaysian ringgit hit a new 42-month low against the dollar on Tuesday, but later recovered as currency players took profits on dollar positions, foreign exchange dealers said.
The ringgit plunged to 2.7930 to a dollar early in the day, its weakest level since February 1994, before rebounding to 2.7645/75 by 1000 GMT.
The ringgit was earlier pressured by persistent dollar demand from offshore funds and weakness in the Singapore dollar, dealers said.

The Singapore dollar fell through the psychological 1.50 to the U.S. dollar level on Tuesday after comments by a Monetary Authority of Singapore official that the currency's level was appropriate to what was happening in the market.
Despite the recovery, dealers said the ringgit remained vulnerable.
Dealers and analysts said the dollar would face some resistance around 2.7950. However, they did not rule out a rise above 2.80 for the first time since dollar/ringgit was officially floated in 1973.
"After recent moves, few would stick their necks out to call for a top at 2.80," said research house MMS International in its market commentary.
"Given that sentiments are overwhelmingly against the ringgit, and the regionals as well, the financial market may well be tempted to create a piece of history," it said.
The ringgit, like other Southeast Asian currencies, has been hit by speculative attacks over the past month, losing nearly 12 percent of its value.
The dollar's rise against the ringgit was also pretty much unchallenged because local exporters have already sold almost all of their dollar positions at 2.67/2.68, dealers said.
"All the indicators are showing an overbought situation, but nobody is looking at the indicators. Everybody out there seems to be buying dollars," a European bank dealer in Singapore said.
"We're staring at 2.80 now. And after that, I have no idea where it could go," said a U.S. bank dealer.
Analysts said there was little justification for the ringgit to fall to its current levels.
The currency has remained under selling pressure since plunging two percent late on Friday shortly after Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said he was happy with the ringgit's level.

Dealers said Mahathir's remarks were taken to mean that the central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia, would allow the ringgit to find its own level and would not intervene to stop the local unit from being sold.
